title: Short Stuff: Morganna the Kissing Bandit
summary: Short Stuff episode on Morganna the Kissing Bandit, the Louisville-born exotic dancer (born Nancy Lee Rose) who became famous in the 1970s and 1980s for running onto Major League Baseball fields and kissing players, along with athletes in other sports. The hosts cover her start with a 1969 bet at Crosley Field involving Pete Rose, her claimed kisses of over fifty athletes, the security beatings that broke her ribs and other bones, her arrest at an Astros game where attorney Richard Haynes proposed a "gravity defense" built on her bust size, her deflection tactics such as the 1986 Don Mattingly fake-out, her cameo in the movie Kingpin, and her retirement and current obscurity.
topics: Hank Aaron home run field rush

segments.title: Introduction to Morganna the Kissing Bandit
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Morganna the Kissing Bandit as a sports-related pop culture figure known for running onto baseball fields in the 1970s and 1980s to kiss players. They note her fame, her exotic dancing career, and her physical attributes, which later come up in court.

segments.title: Early life and the 1969 Crosley Field kiss
segments.summary: Born Nancy Lee Rose in Louisville, Kentucky, she had a rough childhood and was raised partly by her grandfather, who introduced her to baseball. At age seventeen in 1969 at Crosley Field during a Reds game, a friend bet her five dollars to confront Pete Rose, who was endorsing Ballpark Franks. She kissed him on the cheek and returned to her seat, and a Cincinnati sportswriter dubbed her the Kissing Bandit.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Kissing athletes across sports and her prolific career
segments.summary: She kissed athletes in NASCAR, the NBA, the NFL, the NHL, and at a horse race, with George Brett later kissing her on stage at a club as a payback. A Sports Illustrated stat says she kissed over fifty athletes between 1969 and 1999, plus managers, umpires, and mascots. Her presence reportedly doubled stadium crowds, creating a love-hate relationship.

segments.title: Field rushers then and now
segments.summary: The hosts compare her era to later periods, citing Hank Aaron's home run celebration and the 2009 stabbing of Monica Seles as turning points in how security treats people who run onto fields. Today, protesters are often tackled and cameras avoid showing them, while in Morganna's time fans rushing the field were generally seen as harmless.

segments.title: Security beatings and injuries
segments.summary: At the 1970 All-Star Game in Cincinnati, the Reds reportedly put a bounty of one hundred dollars on her capture. Security caught her and kicked her, breaking three ribs. She also reportedly suffered a broken kneecap and a broken tailbone at the hands of security, which she later attributed to overzealous officers.

segments.title: Astros arrest and the gravity defense
segments.summary: She was arrested after rushing the field at an Astros game to kiss Nolan Ryan on the mound and hired attorney Richard Haynes, known as the Racehorse, for her court case. Haynes planned a gravity defense arguing her bust weight would drag her over the railing. The charges were dropped before trial, and the defense became part of her legend.

segments.title: Deflection tactics and later career
segments.summary: She was known for misdirection, such as publicly announcing a 1986 trip to kiss Don Mattingly in New York and instead flying to Seattle to kiss Steve Yeager. Her last recorded kiss was Scottie Pippen in the early 1990s, she had a cameo in the movie Kingpin in 1996, and she officially retired in 2000. She reportedly made millions from her persona.

segments.title: Current whereabouts and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts note that recent information about her is hard to find, that she likely lives in her late seventies though her age is uncertain because she has been untruthful about it, and they wrap up the topic.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the Short Stuff episode and give the standard show credit and podcast information.
